arXiv:1605.02587v2 [math.AP] 26 May 2019

Nodal sets of Laplace eigenfunctions: polynomial upper estimates of the Hausdorff measure.

Alexander Logunov Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv 69978, Israel Address: Chebyshev Laboratory, St. Petersburg State University, 14th Line V.O., 29B, Saint Petersburg 199178 Russia Email address: log239@yandex.ru
Abstract.

Let 𝕄\mathbb{M} be a compact C∞C^{\infty}-smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension nn, n≥3n\geq 3, and let φλ:ΔM​φλ+λ​φλ=0\varphi_{\lambda}:\Delta_{M}\varphi_{\lambda}+\lambda\varphi_{\lambda}=0 denote the Laplace eigenfunction on 𝕄\mathbb{M} corresponding to the eigenvalue λ\lambda. We show that

Hn−1({φλ=0})≤Cλα,H^{n-1}(\{\varphi_{\lambda}=0\})\leq C\lambda^{\alpha},

where α>1/2\alpha>1/2 is a constant, which depends on nn only, and C>0C>0 depends on 𝕄\mathbb{M} . This result is a consequence of our study of zero sets of harmonic functions on C∞C^{\infty}-smooth Riemannian manifolds. We develop a technique of propagation of smallness for solutions of elliptic PDE that allows us to obtain local bounds from above for the volume of the nodal sets in terms of the frequency and the doubling index.

1. Preliminaries

Yau conjectured that the Laplace eigenfunctions φλ:Δ​φλ+λ​φλ=0\varphi_{\lambda}:\Delta\varphi_{\lambda}+\lambda\varphi_{\lambda}=0 on a compact C∞C^{\infty}-smooth Riemannain manifold WW of dimension nn (without boundary) satisfy

cλ1/2≤Hn−1({φλ=0})≤Cλ1/2,c\lambda^{1/2}\leq H^{n-1}(\{\varphi_{\lambda}=0\})\leq C\lambda^{1/2},

where Hn−1​(⋅)H^{n-1}(\cdot) denotes the (n−1)(n-1) dimensional Hausdorf measure, positive constants c,Cc,C depend on the Riemannian metric and on the manifold only. This conjecture was proved for real-analytic manifolds by Donnelly and Fefferman ([5]). For non-analytic manifolds the best-known upper estimate in dimension n=2n=2 was H1({φλ=0})≤Cλ3/4H^{1}(\{\varphi_{\lambda}=0\})\leq C\lambda^{3/4} due to Donnelly and Fefferman ([6]), different proof for the same bound was given by Dong ([4]). Recently this bound was refined to C​λ3/4−εC\lambda^{3/4-\varepsilon} in [12].

In higher dimensions the estimate Hn−1({φλ=0})≤CλC​λH^{n-1}(\{\varphi_{\lambda}=0\})\leq C\lambda^{C\sqrt{\lambda}} by Hardt and Simon ([9]) was the only known upper bound till now. We prove that

Hn−1({φλ=0})≤Cλα,H^{n-1}(\{\varphi_{\lambda}=0\})\leq C\lambda^{\alpha},

where α>1/2\alpha>1/2 is a constant, which depends on nn only, CC depends on MM.

This estimate will follow from an estimate (Theorem 6.1) for harmonic functions, which bounds the volume of the nodal set in terms of the frequency function (or the doubling index).

There is a standard trick that allows to pass from Laplace eigenfunctions to harmonic functions: one can add an extra variable tt and consider a function

u⁡(x,t)=φ⁡(x)​exp⁡(λ​t),u(x,t)=\varphi(x)\exp(\sqrt{\lambda}t),

which appears to be a harmonic function on the product manifold W×ℝW\times\mathbb{R}.

Let MM be a C∞C^{\infty}-smooth Riemannian manifold (non-compact and with no boundary), endowed with metric gg. Consider a point p∈Mp\in M and a harmonic function uu (with respect to gg) on MM. By Bg​(p,r)B_{g}(p,r) we will denote a geodesic ball with center at point pp and radius rr. Define H⁡(r)=∫∂Bg​(p,r)u2​d​SrH(r)=\int\limits_{\partial B_{g}(p,r)}u^{2}dS_{r}, where SrS_{r} is the surface measure on ∂Bg​(p,r)\partial B_{g}(p,r) with respect to gg. We will always assume that rr is smaller than the injectivity radius.

Definition. The frequency function of a harmonic function uu is defined by

β⁡(r):=r​H′​(r)2​H​(r).\beta(r):=\frac{rH^{\prime}(r)}{2H(r)}.

We remark that this definition is slightly different from the standard one, since we don’t normalize H⁡(r)H(r) by the surface measure |Sr||S_{r}|. See [10] for a friendly introduction to frequency and also [8], [11] for applications to nodal sets. In dimension two understanding of nodal sets of harmonic functions is better due to complex analysis techniques and topological reasons, see [16].

We will work only on a bounded subset of MM: fix a point OO on MM and assume hereafter that Bg​(p,r)⊂Bg​(O,1)B_{g}(p,r)\subset B_{g}(O,1).

The frequency is almost monotonic in the following sense (see Remark (3) to Theorem 2.2 in [14]):

Lemma 1.1.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists R0=R0​(ε,M,g,O)R_{0}=R_{0}(\varepsilon,M,g,O) such that

(1) β⁡(r1)≤(1+ε)​β​(r2)\beta(r_{1})\leq(1+\varepsilon)\beta(r_{2})

for any r1,r2r_{1},r_{2}: 0<r1<r2<R00<r_{1}<r_{2}<R_{0}.

One can estimate the growth of H⁡(r)H(r) in terms of the frequency in view of the integral formula:

H⁡(r2)H⁡(r1)=exp⁡(2​∫r1r2β⁡(r)​d​log⁡r).\frac{H(r_{2})}{H(r_{1})}=\exp(2\int_{r_{1}}^{r_{2}}\beta(r)d\log r).
Corollary 1.2.

(r2r1)2​β​(r1)/(1+ε)≤H⁡(r2)H⁡(r1)≤(r2r1)2​β​(r2)​(1+ε)(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}})^{2\beta(r_{1})/(1+\varepsilon)}\leq\frac{H(r_{2})}{H(r_{1})}\leq(\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}})^{2\beta(r_{2})(1+\varepsilon)}.

Sometimes we will specify the center of the ball and our choice of the function uu and write β⁡(p,r)\beta(p,r) and H⁡(p,r)H(p,r) or βu​(p,r)\beta_{u}(p,r) and Hu​(p,r)H_{u}(p,r) in place of β⁡(r)\beta(r) and H⁡(r)H(r).

We need a standard elliptic estimate that compares L∞L^{\infty} and L2L^{2} norms of harmonic functions on concentric geodesic spheres: for any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) there exists a constant C1=C1​(ε,M,g,O)>0C_{1}=C_{1}(\varepsilon,M,g,O)>0 such that

(2) sup∂Bg​(p,r)|u|2≤C1​H⁡(r⁡(1+ε))rn−1\sup\limits_{\partial B_{g}(p,r)}|u|^{2}\leq C_{1}\frac{H(r(1+\varepsilon))}{r^{n-1}}

for r≤R0r\leq R_{0}, where R0=R0​(M,g,O)>0R_{0}=R_{0}(M,g,O)>0.

The reverse estimate holds for arbitrary continuous functions on MM:

(3) H⁡(r)≤C2​(M,g,O)​rn−1​sup∂Bg​(p,r)|u|2,H(r)\leq C_{2}(M,g,O)r^{n-1}\sup\limits_{\partial B_{g}(p,r)}|u|^{2},

where C2​(M,g,O)C_{2}(M,g,O) is a positive constant such that the whole surface measure of a geodesic sphere |Sr|≤rn−1​C2​(M,g)|S_{r}|\leq r^{n-1}C_{2}(M,g), r≤R0r\leq R_{0}.

Let us consider normal coordinates in a geodesic ball Bg​(O,R)B_{g}(O,R), where RR is a sufficiently small number. In these coordinates we will treat the Laplace operator as an elliptic operator in a fixed domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, say, a cube QQ. We will identify OO with the origin and denote the ordinary Euclidean distance by d⁡(x,y)d(x,y) and the Riemannian distance by dg​(x,y)d_{g}(x,y). Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be a small number. We will assume hereafter that

(4) dg​(x,y)d⁡(x,y)∈(1−ε,1+ε)\frac{d_{g}(x,y)}{d(x,y)}\in(1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)

for points x,yx,y in Bg​(O,R0)B_{g}(O,R_{0}): x≠yx\neq y, where R0=R0​(ε,M,g,O)>0R_{0}=R_{0}(\varepsilon,M,g,O)>0. The existence of such R0R_{0} for any ε\varepsilon is provided by the choice of the normal coordinates.

For the purposes of the paper it will be more convenient to work with a notion similar to the frequency: so-called doubling index, which deals with L∞L^{\infty} norms in place of L2L^{2} and Euclidean balls in place of geodesic balls. For a given ball BB (ball in standard Euclidean metric) define the doubling index N⁡(B)N(B) by 2N⁡(B)=sup2​B|u|supB|u|2^{N(B)}=\frac{\sup\limits_{2B}|u|}{\sup\limits_{B}|u|}. Given a positive number rr we denote by r​BrB the homothety image of BB with coefficient rr such that r​BrB and BB have the same center. If BB is an Euclidean ball in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with center at xx and radius rr, then N⁡(x,r)N(x,r) will denote the doubling index for this ball.

We will use the estimates of growth of harmonic functions in terms of the doubling index.

Lemma 1.3.

For any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) there exist C=C⁡(ε,M,g,O)>0C=C(\varepsilon,M,g,O)>0 and R=R⁡(ε,M,g,O)>0R=R(\varepsilon,M,g,O)>0 such that

(5) tN​(x,ρ)​(1−ε)−C≤supB⁡(x,t​ρ)|u|supB⁡(x,ρ)|u|≤tN​(x,t​ρ)​(1+ε)+Ct^{N(x,\rho)(1-\varepsilon)-C}\leq\frac{\sup\limits_{B(x,t\rho)}|u|}{\sup\limits_{B(x,\rho)}|u|}\leq t^{N(x,t\rho)(1+\varepsilon)+C}

for any x∈Mx\in M and numbers ρ>0\rho>0, t>2t>2 satisfying B⁡(x,t​ρ)⊂B⁡(O,R)B(x,t\rho)\subset B(O,R) (and for any harmonic function uu). Furthermore, there exists N0=N0​(ε,M,g)N_{0}=N_{0}(\varepsilon,M,g) such that if additionally N⁡(x,ρ)>N0N(x,\rho)>N_{0}, then

(6) tN​(x,ρ)​(1−ε)≤supB⁡(x,t​ρ)|u|supB⁡(x,ρ)|u|.t^{N(x,\rho)(1-\varepsilon)}\leq\frac{\sup\limits_{B(x,t\rho)}|u|}{\sup\limits_{B(x,\rho)}|u|}.

The estimates (5),(6) are corollaries from almost monotonicity of the frequency (1) and standard elliptic estimates. For the convenience of the reader we deduce them in Lemma 7.2 and Lemma 7.3.

We will show in Theorem 6.1 that there exist r=r⁡(M)>0r=r(M)>0 and α=α⁡(n)>1\alpha=\alpha(n)>1 such that the following inequality holds:

Hn−1({u=0}∩B(O,r))≤C(N(O,Kr))α,H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\cap B(O,r))\leq C(N(O,Kr))^{\alpha},

where K=K⁡(n)≥2K=K(n)\geq 2 and C=C⁡(M)C=C(M).

Note that for real analytic manifolds one can replace α\alpha by 11 in the estimate above, using complex analysis techniques (holomorhpic extension of a harmonic function to an open set in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} and Jensen’s formula on one dimensional sections), see [8].

We remark that only few properties of Hn−1H^{n-1} are used in the proof: subadditivity and the rescaling property. So there is a chance that the methods of this paper might be applied to other characteristics of nodal sets.

We outline the question we are trying to investigate in this paper: Is the frequency additive in some sense?

Some partial positive answers are obtained in the simplex lemma and in the hyperplane lemma, which are combined to get the polynomial upper bounds for the volume of the nodal sets in terms of the frequency (or the doubling index).

2. Simplex lemma

Let x1,…,xn+1x_{1},\dots,x_{n+1} be vertices of a simplex SS in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The symbol d​i​a​m​(S)diam(S) will denote the diameter of SS and by w​i​d​t​h​(S)width(S) we will denote the width of SS, i.e. the minimum distance between a pair of parallel hyperplanes such that SS is contained between them. Define the relative width of SS: w⁡(S)=w​i​d​t​h​(S)/d​i​a​m​(S)w(S)=width(S)/diam(S). Let a>0a>0 and assume that w⁡(S)>aw(S)>a. In particular we assume that x1,…,xn+1x_{1},\dots,x_{n+1} do not lie on the same hyperplane. For the purposes of the paper there will be sufficient a particular choice of aa, which depends on the dimension nn only, the choice will be specified in Section 5. Denote by x0x_{0} the barycenter of SS.

We will use an Euclidean geometry lemma: there exist c1>0c_{1}>0, K≥2/aK\geq 2/a depending on a,na,n only such that if ρ=K​d​i​a​m​(S)\rho=Kdiam(S), then B(x0,ρ(1+c1))⊂∪i=1n+1B(xi,ρ)B(x_{0},\rho(1+c_{1}))\subset\cup_{i=1}^{n+1}B(x_{i},\rho).

We remark that if the simplex is very degenerate (aa is small), then c1c_{1} has to be small and the number KK has to be big:

c1→0,K→+∞​ as ​a→0.c_{1}\to 0,K\to+\infty\textup{ as }a\to 0.
Lemma 2.1.

Let BiB_{i} be balls with centers at xix_{i} and radii not greater than K2​d​i​a​m​(S)\frac{K}{2}diam(S), i=1,…,n+1i=1,\dots,n+1, where K=K⁡(a,n)K=K(a,n) is from the Euclidean geometry lemma. There exist positive numbers c=c⁡(a,n)c=c(a,n), C=C⁡(a,n)≥KC=C(a,n)\geq K, r=r⁡(M,g,O,a)r=r(M,g,O,a), N0=N0​(M,g,O,a)N_{0}=N_{0}(M,g,O,a) such that if S⊂B⁡(O,r)S\subset B(O,r) and if N⁡(Bi)>NN(B_{i})>N for each xix_{i}, i=1​…​n+1i=1\dots{n+1}, where NN is a number greater than N0N_{0}, then N⁡(x0,C​d​i​a​m​(S))>N⁡(1+c)N(x_{0},Cdiam(S))>N(1+c).

Proof.

In view of almost monotonicity of the doubling index (5) we will assume that all BiB_{i} have the same radius ρ=K​d​i​a​m​(S)\rho=Kdiam(S).

Let MM be the supremum of |u||u| over the union of B⁡(xi,ρ)B(x_{i},\rho), then |u||u| is not greater than MM in B⁡(x0,ρ⁡(1+c1))B(x_{0},\rho(1+c_{1})) and supB⁡(xi,ρ)|u|=M\sup\limits_{B(x_{i},\rho)}|u|=M for some ii. Let t>2t>2 and ε>0\varepsilon>0, these parameters will be specified later. Assume that (6) holds for B⁡(xi,ρ​t)B(x_{i},\rho t), then supB⁡(xi,ρ​t)|u|≥M​tN⁡(1−ε)\sup\limits_{B(x_{i},\rho t)}|u|\geq Mt^{N(1-\varepsilon)}.

We need a metric geometry fact, which follows from the triangle inequality: there exists δ=δ⁡(t)∈(0,1)\delta=\delta(t)\in(0,1) such that B⁡(xi,ρ​t)⊂B⁡(x0,ρ​t​(1+δ))B(x_{i},\rho t)\subset B(x_{0},\rho t(1+\delta)) and δ⁡(t)→0\delta(t)\to 0 as t→+∞t\to+\infty.

Hence

for some c2=c2​(t,c1)∈(0,1)c_{2}=c_{2}(t,c_{1})\in(0,1). Second, we choose ε=ε⁡(c2)>0\varepsilon=\varepsilon(c_{2})>0 and c=c⁡(c2)>0c=c(c_{2})>0 such that

t(1−c2)​(N~​(1+ε)+C)≥tN⁡(1−ε).t^{(1-c_{2})(\widetilde{N}(1+\varepsilon)+C)}\geq t^{N(1-\varepsilon)}.

We therefore have

3. Propagation of smallness of the Cauchy data

If one considers a smooth Riemannian metric gg in a unit cube QQ in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, then any harmonic function uu (with respect to gg) satisfies L​u=0Lu=0, where LL is a uniformly elliptic (in a slightly smaller cube) operator of second order in the divergence form with smooth coefficients. Consider a cube q⊂12​Qq\subset\frac{1}{2}Q with side rr and let FF be a face of qq. In this section we formulate a result that we will refer to as the propagation of smallness of the Cauchy data for elliptic PDE. See Lemma 4.3 in [11] and Theorem 1.7 in [1] for the proof of the result below, which we bring not in full generality but in a convenient way for our purposes.

Suppose that |u|≤1|u|\leq 1 in qq. There exist C>0C>0 and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), depending on LL only such that if |u|≤ε|u|\leq\varepsilon on FF and |∇u|≤εr|\nabla u|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{r} on FF, ε<1\varepsilon<1, then

(10) sup12​q|u|≤C​εα.\sup\limits_{\frac{1}{2}q}|u|\leq C\varepsilon^{\alpha}.
Remark 3.1.

We will apply propagation of smallness of the Cauchy data in the case when the coefficients of the operator LL are sufficiently close in the L∞L^{\infty} norm to the coefficients of the standard Laplace operator Δ\Delta in B⁡(O,R0)B(O,R_{0}) and the derivatives of coefficients LL are sufficiently small. Under these assumptions α\alpha can be chosen to depend only on nn, see Theorem 1.7 in [1].

4. Hyperplane lemma

Given a cube QQ, we will denote supx∈Q,r∈(0,d​i​a​m​(Q))N⁡(x,r)\sup\limits_{x\in Q,r\in(0,diam(Q))}N(x,r) by N⁡(Q)N(Q) and call it the doubling index of QQ. This definition is different than a doubling index for balls but more convenient in the following sense. If a cube qq is contained in a cube QQ, then N⁡(q)≤N⁡(Q)N(q)\leq N(Q). Furthermore if a cube qq is covered by cubes QiQ_{i} with d​i​a​m​(Qi)≥d​i​a​m​(q)diam(Q_{i})\geq diam(q), then N⁡(Qi)≥N⁡(q)N(Q_{i})\geq N(q) for some QiQ_{i}.

Lemma 4.1.

Let QQ be a cube [−R,R]n[-R,R]^{n} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Divide QQ into (2​A+1)n(2A+1)^{n} equal subcubes qiq_{i} with side-length 2​R2​A+1\frac{2R}{2A+1}. Consider the cubes qi,0q_{i,0} that have non-empty intersection with the hyperplane xn=0x_{n}=0. Suppose that for each qi,0q_{i,0} there exists xi∈qi,0x_{i}\in q_{i,0} and ri<10​d​i​a​m​(qi,0)r_{i}<10diam(q_{i,0}) such that N⁡(xi,ri)>NN(x_{i},r_{i})>N, where NN is a given positive number. Then there exist A0=A0​(n)A_{0}=A_{0}(n), R0=R0​(M,g,O)R_{0}=R_{0}(M,g,O), N0=N0​(M,g,O)N_{0}=N_{0}(M,g,O) such that if A>A0A>A_{0}, N>N0N>N_{0}, R<R0R<R_{0} then N⁡(Q)>2​NN(Q)>2N.

Proof.

We will ask R0R_{0} to be small enough so that Lemma 1.3 holds with ε=1/2\varepsilon=1/2 and 10​n⋅R010n\cdot R_{0} in place of RR in Lemma 1.3. Also we may assume that coefficients of LL are close to the coefficients of the standard Laplacian in C1​(B⁡(O,10​n⋅R0))C^{1}(B(O,10n\cdot R_{0})) to be able to use (10). We have described our choice of R0R_{0}.

For the sake of simplicity we will assume that R=1/2R=1/2 and R0≥1/2R_{0}\geq 1/2. The general case follows by changing the scale in the argument below.

Let BB be the unit ball B⁡(O,1)B(O,1) and let MM be the supremum of uu over 18​B\frac{1}{8}B. For each xix_{i} in 116​B\frac{1}{16}B the ball B⁡(xi,1/32)B(x_{i},1/32) is contained in 1/8​B1/8B. Hence supB⁡(xi,1/32)|u|≤M\sup\limits_{B(x_{i},1/32)}|u|\leq M. Using N⁡(xi,ri)>NN(x_{i},r_{i})>N and (5) with ε=1/2\varepsilon=1/2 we get

sup2​qi,0|u|≤supB⁡(xi,4​n2​A+1)|u|≤C​supB⁡(xi,1/32)|u|​(128​n2​A+1)N2≤M​2−c​N​log⁡A,\sup\limits_{2q_{i,0}}|u|\leq\sup\limits_{B(x_{i},\frac{4\sqrt{n}}{2A+1})}|u|\leq C\sup\limits_{B(x_{i},1/32)}|u|\left(\frac{128\sqrt{n}}{2A+1}\right)^{\frac{N}{2}}\leq M2^{-cN\log A},

where c=c⁡(n)>0c=c(n)>0. In the last inequality we assumed that A>A0​(n)A>A_{0}(n) and NN is sufficiently large .

By a standard elliptic estimate

supqi,0|∇u|≤C​A​sup2​qi,0|u|≤C​A​M​2−c​N​log⁡A≤M​2−c1​(n)​N​log⁡A.\sup\limits_{q_{i,0}}|\nabla u|\leq CA\sup\limits_{2q_{i,0}}|u|\leq CAM2^{-cN\log A}\leq M2^{-c_{1}(n)N\log A}.

Corollary 4.2.

Fix a cube Qi1,i2,…,ij=:qQ_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{j}}=:q, we are interested in the number of its bad subcubes Qi1,i2,…,ij+1=:qij+1Q_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{j+1}}=:q_{i_{j+1}}. 6. Upper estimates of the volume of the nodal set.

Theorem 6.1.

There exist positive numbers r=r⁡(M,g,O)r=r(M,g,O), C=C⁡(M,g,O)C=C(M,g,O) and α=α⁡(n)\alpha=\alpha(n) such that for any harmonic function uu on MM and any cube Q⊂B⁡(O,r)Q\subset B(O,r)

(11) Hn−1({u=0}∩Q)≤Cdiamn−1(Q)Nuα(Q),H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\cap Q)\leq Cdiam^{n-1}(Q)N_{u}^{\alpha}(Q),

where Nu​(Q)N_{u}(Q) is the doubling index of QQ for the function uu.

Proof.

Choose rr so that Theorem 5.1 holds with this rr and some c=c⁡(n)c=c(n), A=A⁡(n)A=A(n). Now, define the function

F⁡(N):=supHn−1({u=0}∩Q)d​i​a​mn−1​(Q),F(N):=\sup\frac{H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\cap Q)}{diam^{n-1}(Q)},

where the supremum is taken over the set of harmonic functions uu on MM, which we denote by Harm​(M)\textup{Harm}(M), and cubes QQ within B⁡(O,r)B(O,r) such that Nu​(Q)≤NN_{u}(Q)\leq N. The estimate (11) is equivalent to

(12) F⁡(N)≤C​Nα.F(N)\leq CN^{\alpha}.

We note that if uu changes a sign in QQ, then Nu​(Q)≥1N_{u}(Q)\geq 1, since limt→+0N⁡(x,t)\lim\limits_{t\to+0}N(x,t) is equal to the vanishing order of uu at xx. Due to the Hardt-Simon exponential bounds we know F⁡(N)<+∞F(N)<+\infty for each positive NN.

We will call N>0N>0 bad if

(13) F⁡(N)>4​A⋅F⁡(N/(1+c)).F(N)>4A\cdot F(N/(1+c)).

Our goal is to show that the set of bad NN is bounded. In view of monotonicity of FF it would imply (12) immediately, where the constant α\alpha depends on AA and cc only and therefore only on the dimension nn.

Consider a bad NN and a function uu with a cube QQ such that F⁡(N)F(N) is almost attained for them:

(14) Hn−1({u=0}∩Q)d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)>34​F​(N)\frac{H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\cap Q)}{diam^{n-1}(Q)}>\frac{3}{4}F(N)

while Nu​(Q)≤NN_{u}(Q)\leq N. Divide QQ into AnA^{n} equal subcubes QiQ_{i}, i=1,…,Ani=1,\dots,A^{n}. ≤|G1|F⁡(N)​d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)An−1+|G2|​F​(N/(1+c))​d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)An−1=I+I​I.\leq|G_{1}|F(N)\frac{diam^{n-1}(Q)}{A^{n-1}}+|G_{2}|F(N/(1+c))\frac{diam^{n-1}(Q)}{A^{n-1}}=I+II.

Since |G1|≤12​An−1|G_{1}|\leq\frac{1}{2}A^{n-1} we can estimate I≤12​F​(N)​d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)I\leq\frac{1}{2}F(N)diam^{n-1}(Q). Using that NN is bad, we have I​I≤|G2|​F⁡(N)4​A​d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)An−1II\leq|G_{2}|\frac{F(N)}{4A}\frac{diam^{n-1}(Q)}{A^{n-1}} and |G2|≤An|G_{2}|\leq A^{n}, hence I​I≤14​F​(N)​d​i​a​mn−1​(Q)II\leq\frac{1}{4}F(N)diam^{n-1}(Q). Finally, Hn−1({u=0}∩Q)≤34F(N)diamn−1(Q)H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\cap Q)\leq\frac{3}{4}F(N)diam^{n-1}(Q) and the last inequality contradicts to (14). Theorem 6.2.

Let (W,g)(W,g) be a compact C∞C^{\infty}-smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary. For a Laplace eigenfunction φ\varphi on WW with Δ​φ+λ​φ=0\Delta\varphi+\lambda\varphi=0 define its nodal set Zφ:={φ=0}Z_{\varphi}:=\{\varphi=0\}. There exist C=C⁡(W,g)C=C(W,g) and α\alpha, depending only on the dimension nn of WW, such that

Hn−1​(Zφ)≤C​λα.H^{n-1}(Z_{\varphi})\leq C\lambda^{\alpha}.
Proof.

We will use a standard trick that allows to pass from Laplace eigenfunctions to harmonic functions by adding an extra variable. Consider a product manifold M=W×ℝM=W\times\mathbb{R}, where one can define a harmonic function uu by

u⁡(x,t)=φ⁡(x)​eλ⋅t,x∈W,t∈ℝ.u(x,t)=\varphi(x)e^{\sqrt{\lambda}\cdot t},x\in W,t\in\mathbb{R}.

The Donnelly-Fefferman doubling index estimate for Laplace eigenfunctions claims

supBg​(p,2​r)|φ|≤2C​λ​supBg​(p,r)|φ|,\sup\limits_{B_{g}(p,2r)}|\varphi|\leq 2^{C\sqrt{\lambda}}\sup\limits_{B_{g}(p,r)}|\varphi|,

where C=C⁡(M,g)C=C(M,g), pp is any point on WW and r∈(0,R0​(M,g))r\in(0,R_{0}(M,g)). It implies that the doubling index of uu is also bounded by C1​λC_{1}\sqrt{\lambda} in balls with radius smaller than some R1=R1​(W,g)R_{1}=R_{1}(W,g). Let us fix a point O∈MO\in M and a point O~=(O,0)∈M\widetilde{O}=(O,0)\in M. We can apply Theorem 6.1 to see that Hn({u=0}∩B(O~,r))≤C2λαH^{n}(\{u=0\}\cap B(\widetilde{O},r))\leq C_{2}\lambda^{\alpha} for some r=r⁡(W,g)>0r=r(W,g)>0.

It remains to note that Hn({u=0}∩B(O~,r))≤C2λαH^{n}(\{u=0\}\cap B(\widetilde{O},r))\leq C_{2}\lambda^{\alpha} implies Hn−1({φ=0}∩Bg(O,r/2))≤C3λαH^{n-1}(\{\varphi=0\}\cap B_{g}(O,r/2))\leq C_{3}\lambda^{\alpha} since the zero set of uu is exactly Zφ×ℝZ_{\varphi}\times\mathbb{R}. Finally, one can cover MM by finite number of such balls and obtain the desired global estimate of the volume of the nodal set. ∎

Remark. The same argument gives a local volume estimate of the nodal set:

Hn−1({φ=0}∩Bg(O,r))≤Crn−1λα.H^{n-1}(\{\varphi=0\}\cap B_{g}(O,r))\leq Cr^{n-1}\lambda^{\alpha}.

Lemma 7.1.

If ε1>0\varepsilon_{1}>0 is a sufficiently small number (ε1<1/1010\varepsilon_{1}<1/10^{10}), then there exist C=C⁡(ε1,M,g,O)>0C=C(\varepsilon_{1},M,g,O)>0 and R1=R1​(ε1,M,g,O)>0R_{1}=R_{1}(\varepsilon_{1},M,g,O)>0 such that
